settings: Each prompt is a fresh call with a short survey-style system prompt; 3 runs, both option orders; reasoning effort low, max 2,000 tokens, via OpenRouter, November 2026.

asian_disease.label: Lives saved vs. lives lost
asian_disease.measure: Extra share picking the sure option when it's described as lives saved (points)
asian_disease.people: 72% picked the sure option when it was described as lives saved, 22% when described as lives lost.
asian_disease.asked: A disease will kill 600 people. Pick a sure plan or a gamble. Half the participants hear the plans described as lives saved, half as lives lost.
asian_disease.effect: Framing: the same options feel safer when described as gains and riskier when described as losses.

changes.isomorph: Same numbers and thirds, but factory jobs instead of a disease.
changes.new_numbers: Same disease story, with 900 people instead of 600.
changes.deep: An orchard of 120 trees, a 37.5% chance instead of one third, and "treatments" instead of programs.

lost_ticket.label: Lost cash vs. lost ticket
lost_ticket.measure: Extra share buying a ticket after losing cash than after losing the ticket (points)
lost_ticket.people: 88% would still buy a ticket after losing $10 cash; 46% after losing the $10 ticket.
lost_ticket.asked: You arrive at a play and find you've lost $10. Do you still buy a $10 ticket? Others are told they lost the $10 ticket they had already bought.
lost_ticket.effect: Mental accounting: losing a ticket feels like paying twice; losing cash doesn't.

changes.isomorph: A museum exhibition instead of a play; still $10.
changes.new_numbers: An $80 concert instead of a $10 play.
changes.deep: A $45 climbing-gym day pass, booked for the wrong day instead of lost.

jacket_calculator.label: Saving $5 on a cheap vs. an expensive item
jacket_calculator.measure: Extra share making the trip when the saving is on the cheap item (points)
jacket_calculator.people: 68% would drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a $15 item; 29% to save $5 on a $125 item.
jacket_calculator.asked: A $15 calculator is $5 cheaper at a store 20 minutes away. Do you go? Others hear the same $5 saving on a $125 calculator.
jacket_calculator.effect: Relative thinking: $5 feels like more when it's a big share of the price.

organ_default.label: Defaults
organ_default.measure: Extra share choosing the option when it's pre-selected (points)
organ_default.people: About 82% stayed organ donors when that was the default; about 42% opted in when it wasn't.
organ_default.asked: You've moved to a new state. Being an organ donor is either already selected or not, and you can change it with one click. What do you choose?
organ_default.effect: Defaults: people tend to keep whatever is pre-selected.

changes.isomorph: Renewing a driver's license online instead of moving; still organ donation.
changes.deep: A $4-a-month towel service on a gym sign-up form instead of organ donation.

anchoring.label: Anchoring on a random number
anchoring.measure: Anchoring index: how far the estimate moves, as a share of the gap between the two anchors
anchoring.people: After a wheel stopped at 10 or 65, median guesses were 25% and 45% (index 0.36).
anchoring.asked: A wheel of fortune lands on 10 (or 65). Is the share of African countries in the UN higher or lower than that number? Then give your best estimate.
anchoring.effect: Anchoring: an irrelevant number pulls the estimate toward it.

endowment.label: Owning something makes it worth more
endowment.measure: Selling price ÷ buying price (1 = no gap)
endowment.people: Mug owners asked a median $7.12; non-owners offered $2.87 (ratio 2.48).
endowment.asked: You've just been given a mug: what's the least you'd sell it for? Others, without a mug, say the most they'd pay for one.
endowment.effect: Endowment: owning something makes it feel worth more.

loss_aversion.label: Losses loom larger
loss_aversion.measure: Smallest acceptable win ÷ the loss, on a 50-50 bet (1 = no loss aversion)
loss_aversion.people: Most people want to win about twice what they could lose (ratio about 2).
loss_aversion.asked: A coin flip: tails you lose $100, heads you win $X. What's the smallest X that makes you take the bet?
loss_aversion.effect: Loss aversion: a loss hurts about twice as much as an equal gain feels good.

prospect.label: Choosing between gambles
prospect.measure: Average gap to the share of people picking each option (points; 0 = matches people)
prospect.people: Kahneman & Tversky's 1979 problems: the certainty effect, the reflection effect and the fourfold pattern.
prospect.asked: Pairs of gambles, such as an 80% chance of $4,000 or $3,000 for sure, and the same as losses.
prospect.effect: Certainty and reflection: people play safe with gains and gamble to avoid a sure loss.

changes.isomorph: The same gamble as sealed envelopes in a radio prize draw.
changes.deep: A hotel store credit: 90% of $560 or $480 for sure.

regret_action.label: Regret: acting vs. not acting
regret_action.measure: Gap to the share of people picking each person (points; 0 = matches people)
regret_action.people: 92% said the person who acted (switched stocks) feels worse.
regret_action.asked: Paul kept his stock and George switched; both ended up $1,200 worse off. Who feels worse?
regret_action.effect: Regret for actions: a bad result you caused by acting stings more than one you let happen.

regret_exception.label: Regret: breaking a routine
regret_exception.measure: Gap to the share of people picking each person (points; 0 = matches people)
regret_exception.people: 88% said the person who broke their routine feels worse.
regret_exception.asked: Mr. Jones rarely picks up hitchhikers and Mr. Smith often does. Both gave a ride and were robbed. Who regrets it more?
regret_exception.effect: Regret for exceptions: a bad result after breaking your routine stings more.

He now learns that he would have been better off by $1,200 if he had kept his stock in company B. Who feels greater regret?

canonical.stem: Imagine that the U.S. is preparing for the outbreak of an unusual Asian disease, which is expected to kill 600 people. Two alternative programs to combat the disease have been proposed. Assume that the exact scientific estimates of the consequences of the programs are as follows. Which program would you favor?
canonical.option_a: If this one is adopted, 200 people will be saved.
canonical.option_b: If this one is adopted, there is a one-third probability that all 600 people will be saved and a two-thirds probability that no people will be saved.

deep.stem: Your neighborhood's community orchard has 120 apple trees, and a fungal blight has reached it. Without treatment every tree will die this season. An arborist offers two treatments and says her estimates are reliable. As a member of the orchard committee, which do you vote for?
deep.option_a: Treatment Q: 45 of the 120 trees will be saved.
deep.option_b: Treatment R: a 37.5% chance that all 120 trees will be saved, and a 62.5% chance that none will be saved.

canonical.stem: A wheel of fortune with numbers from 0 to 100 was just spun in front of you and stopped at 65. First: is the percentage of African nations among the members of the United Nations higher or lower than 65? Then give your best estimate of the percentage of African nations among the members of the United Nations.

deep.stem: You are filling in a volunteer form at your local library. The first box asks for your locker number, and you write 88. The next box asks: "Roughly how many books do you think this branch lends out on a typical day?" What number do you write?

canonical.stem: Imagine that you are about to buy a jacket for $125 and a calculator for $15. The salesperson tells you that the calculator you wish to buy is on sale for $10 at the other branch of the store, a 20-minute drive away. Would you make the trip to the other store?

deep.stem: You are at an electronics store buying a laptop for $1,200 and a protective case for $30. A friend texts that the exact same case is $20 at a shop a 15-minute walk away. Do you walk over to buy the case there?

caveats: 6 answers per question (3 repeats × both option orders). One answer either way moves a rate by about 17 points. Repeated calls to one model measure how much its answers vary, not a population of people.
Zero-width intervals mean the model answered the same way every time, not that the value is exact: 0 out of 6 is still compatible with a true rate up to about 39%.

Only the original wordings have measured human data; the other versions assume people would answer the same way. The organ-default rates were read from a figure, and Paul and George has no published sample size.
One disguise per effect, one system prompt and one reasoning effort (low). Any single story could have its own quirks.
Claude only: three sizes of one family, so the patterns may not hold for other labs' models.
"Names the study" is a keyword search of the answer text, so it's approximate.
